• Figure1 – It is difficult to correctly interpret the evolution of S- and p- contributions with temperature as they include both, the temperature dependence of the molecular contributions to the surface tension (given in the SI) and the temperature dependent population ratios. The latter are given in figure 1b, however, only for bulk water. There is as far as I could see no graph presented that shows the temperature dependent population ratio between S- and p-state water for the relevant interfacial region. It would be very helpful to the reader if the authors could include such a figure.

• Page 3 – in the first paragraph, the authors refer to the “thermal Marangoni effect”. It would be more appropriate to refer to this as the “Bénard–Marangoni effect”.

• Page 3 – The authors discuss the origin of the relatively high surface tension of air-water, attributing it to the “strong electrostatic interactions and the directional nature of hydrogen bonds”. I think it would be worth clarifying that the bond energy of the hydrogen bonds, in relation to other intermolecular interactions, is also a substantial factor here given that the surface tension represents a surface energy density that is contributed to by the loss in H-bonding.

• Figure 2 – In this figure, as well as in the text, the density is given the symbol ρ. As this is also used for one of the two states of water (ρ-state), I would recommend the authors change one or the other for better clarity.

• Figure 2 – I think the comparison between the plots in Figure 2 with those in Figures S2-S6 could perhaps benefit from consistent axis scaling.

• Figure 2 – For clarity, I think it would perhaps be clearer to not use black and blue for the pressure contributions in the inset to part (d) given that these are used to represent the total and s-state contributions elsewhere in the figure. The same obviously applies to figures S2-S6.

• Page 8 – the authors claim that the anisotropy extends “10 Å below the interface”. I think two points of clarification are warranted here. Firstly, describing it as extending “below” the interface is perhaps somewhat misleading given that this 3D region somehow defines the interface. This length-scale is often described relative to the Gibbs-dividing-surface (GDS), but this exists part-way through this anisotropic region. Secondly, this value of 10 Å is higher than values quoted elsewhere, particularly in relation to the structural anisotropy probed by second-order optical methods. For example, the DFT-based MD simulations in ref. 57 show only ~two contributing ‘layers’ or around 3.5 Å. Alternatively, other recent MD simulations using MB-pol along with experimental measurements using second-order optics concluded around 6-8 Å [Langmuir 2024, 40, 35, 18760–18772]. It would be helpful to the reader if the authors put their obtained value into the context of these other measurements, particularly highlighting why their value might differ with it being not based on the structural anisotropy probed by second-order methods.

• Page 8 – I find the last paragraph generally lacking in clarity and justification. For example, it is not clear to me why the stress anisotropy should be quantified by the maximum peak in the γw profile – is this not essentially only considering the molecules with the largest contribution to the surface tension at the expense of the (like more numerous) other contributors? It is also not clear to me what the justification is for attributing the sharp rise in stress anisotropy for the S-state to the orientational ordering at low T. I think general readers would benefit from additional clarification in this section.

• Page 9 – I think the explanation for why the competition between enhancement of Δs due to the negative pressure and the enhancement of OH ordering leads to the essentially constant, but inward shifting peak position needs more clarity. Unless I am mistaken, the increase in OH ordering essentially contributes negatively to Δs, while the negative pressure contributes positively to it. Therefore, if both increase equally, no change in the profile should occur. The fact that the peak position is shifted to lower z-positions whilst maintaining the overall peak height then suggests not only a change in amplitude of these two factors, but also in their depth-dependence.

• Page 9 and Figure 3 – The authors should clarify the definition of Δs. On page 9 it is defined as the difference between the peak and the bulk value, therefore being independent on z, while in figure 3 it is defined differently as s(z) – s bulk. Based on the discussion on page 9 about having a constant Δs for different temperatures, the former definition seems to be more appropriate. Therefore, the authors should change figure 3(a) and its caption accordingly.

• Figure 3 – I find parts (d) and (e) here not at all clear in terms of what they are trying to display / show. I suggest the authors make changes to this figure to make it clearer the purpose of these sub-figures.

• Figure 4 – In addition to figures 5, 6, S8, and S9, I think the way the structural motifs of different molecules are presented by showing the 2D plots of one O-H angle vs. the other are not at all intuitive. This is largely due to the non-independent relationship between the two angles. A good example of this is the isotropic distribution shown in Figure 4(f). When one thinks of an isotropic distribution in terms of molecular orientations, one naturally imagines a perfectly smooth plane where all orientations are equal. With this cos(θ 1) vs cos(θ 2) way of showing the orientations, this isotropic picture is far from what is obtained. It seems to me that the desired structural information could equally be obtained by describing the structures in terms of their two independent Euler angles: tilt of the molecular dipole, and twist around the dipolar axis. This description can be found in recent simulation work on the air-water interface by the Netz group [arXiv:2505.12962 and arXiv:2505.19856]. With such a description, the isotropic distribution yields a perfectly smooth image that seems much more intuitive to the reader. Therefore, while I realize that a reasonably large effort is required in changing the figures from the current description to the tilt-twist description, I think it would be highly valuable for the understanding and general readability of the paper. It also has the additional benefit that the tilt angle then describes perfectly the distribution of dipole orientations.

• Page 11 – I think the authors should refine their statement on the water orientation at the interface. Currently, they state that “the OH bonds in the top layer orient upward towards air”. While I agree that similar statements are often used to describe the air-water interface, this is not an accurate representation. Instead, the top layer has an average dipole orientation pointing towards air, but nevertheless has a broad distribution. Therefore, simply stating that the OH bonds point towards air is overstating the population of these moieties. Furthermore, as shown in the orientational profiles, the most populated structural motif in the ‘top layer’ is something akin to #2, which only has a single of its OH groups directed towards air. The statement as it stands, however, makes it sound like both OH groups are pointing towards air, more akin to structure #1. While these may seem like subtle points, it completely changes the ‘picture’ of the interfacial structure’

• Page 12 – The authors discuss the non-negligible proportion of in-plane water molecules. Firstly, I find it very difficult with the current way this is presented (see above comment) as well as the chosen color-scale to identify this “non-negligible” population. As above, I recommend that the authors present this differently. Secondly, the authors discuss the energetic favorability of the in-plane structural motif, but make no contrast to other thermodynamic factors. After all, the in-plane structures seem not to be the dominant orientation, so if they are energetically favorable compared to pointing up/down dipoles, the authors need to clearly qualify why they are not the predominant structure.

• Page 13 – The authors state that they “detect a significant number of water molecules displaying structures indicative of dipole alignment”. I would again suggest that this can be more clearly shown with the tilt-twist description given that the distribution of tilt vs z perfectly describes the extend of dipolar alignment.

• Page 13 – The authors state that the “S-state consistently exhibits less pronounced OH-orientational order, characterised by a more dispersed P(cos(θ 1), cos(θ 2))”. Firstly, I don’t think this is immediately obvious from the figures in the way they are currently presented. Take for example Figure 5(a) and (f). It is hard to qualitatively compare the orientational order simply by looking at these two plots. There should be a way to better quantify this and provide a more robust statement on this point. Secondly, the disperse nature of P(cos(θ 1), cos(θ 2)) is not automatically connected to orientational order. An example of this is a distribution with two preferred, but different, orientations. This can make it seem more disperse while actually the extent of the orientational order could be very high.

• Figure 7 – In parts (e) and (f), don’t use pink as the color for 16-17Å since this color represents 21-22Å in (c) and (d), with all the other colors being consistent.

• Figure 9 – The authors state that “it is evident that the S-state is particularly favoured in forming 5-, 6-, and 7-membered rings,…”. Given that f S < f ρ I would suggest rewording this as the rings are actually strictly favored by the ρ-state. Unless I am mistaken, what the authors mean here is that the 4-membered ring state is the only state showing a lower population than the average, indicating it is less energetically favorable than the average s-environment.

• Page 16 – when discussing the orientational distributions of the H-bonded O-Hs, the authors show that it is a broad, symmetric distribution around 0. Firstly, I am surprised that the distribution is symmetric. Given the asymmetry of the z-dependent anisotropy at the interface, I would naturally expect the distribution to reflect this. Perhaps the authors could add a comment on this. Secondly, the authors state that these distributions indicate a “low probability of being dangling”. I find this somewhat of an irrelevant statement since they are discussing the orientational distribution of H-bonded O-H groups, i.e. one should expect that they are not ‘dangling’ simply by definition.

• Page 17 – The authors claim that they “find that the S-state is more favourable for the formation of these nucleation precursors”. I would argue on the contrary as the ρ-state has far higher f-fractions for the ring structures. I therefore think that the authors should expand on this point.

• Page 20 – In the conclusions, the authors propose the possibility of validating these simulation results using second-order spectroscopy methods. I completely agree that this would be a valuable approach to test the proposed structural mechanism. As such, it would also be interesting to calculate the depth-dependent χ(2) in such low temperature conditions, particularly splitting the contributions for the s-state and ρ-state water. This would give clear indicators for the potential of future experimental measurements. While I guess this is beyond the scope of this work, it might be useful to comment on this as future potential.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript Tanaka and co-workers have examined the behavior of the surface tension of the air-water interface in an effort to rationalize/explain its apparent anomalous behavior under supercooling. While the experimental literature observation on this remains inconclusive, there have been several suggestions/indications on the existence of an inflection point in the surface tension and its relationship to thermodynamic anomalies.
While the paper tackles an interesting problem in the physical-chemistry/chemical-physics of liquid water and at aqueous interfaces, I am not entirely convinced about its urgency or broad impact. I believe it sits much better in a more specialized/technical journal like JCP or JPC. In fact, the authors site a previous paper on the topic published in JCP - while the approaches are different, the two works mirror each other quite closely (https://pubs.aip.org/aip/jcp/article/158/5/054503/2871767/High-density-liquid-HDL-adsorption-at-the). Specifically, the paper uses standard models (TIP4P) and standard analysis tools - rings, parameters that have been pioneered by Tanaka. All very interesting, but still standard and would find a better place in specialized journal.
I now raise my specific issues with the paper which I hope will be useful for the authors for a future publication elsewhere:
1) The authors use TIP4P/2005 water model. This is fine and perfectly okay. How much do their results translate to another more accurate model such as MB-pol. I am not suggesting they repeat all their analysis with MB-pol but some discussion on the limitations are needed. Furthermore, some benchmarks with a polarizable model would also make a much more convincing case.
2) More conceptually, I am really not convinced by the s-vs-p state water partitioning that is done here. It seems like a real desire to fit into previous two-state models of water invoked to try to rationalize the putative second critical point of water/and anomalies. In particular, have the authors looked at the dynamics (correlation function) associated with the theta and eta parameters that they claim yield a two-state underlying thermodynamics. Related to this point, the authors should prove using a committor analysis that they have the correct free energy landscape - Figure 1b. Until these dynamical properties are examined which can unequivocally show the two-state behavior the arguments cannot be used to rationalize the fluctuations at the air-water interface.
3) Related to point 2), there have been several studies challenging the notion of 2-state water at least at room temperature and in particular the sensitivity of the results to the choice of collective variable/order parameter - the authors should look and comment on the following papers - https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jctc.1c01292, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpcb.2c07169, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jctc.2c01205, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpclett.4c00383).
4) Related to my previous point - what is known from SFG spectroscopy on the water orientations as a function of supercooling? I know the authors look at the dipole orientations and make some connections with SFG data - however, wouldn't a simpler argument for all this analysis simply be rooted in fluctuations in one free energy minimum that shifts as a function of temperature?
5) I have not done a thorough literature review but I think there are papers that should be examined more carefully on the topic of surface tension and how it changes under supercooling - on such paper that is missing from the current paper are the following - https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.jpclett.0c01163, https://pubs.aip.org/aip/jcp/article-abstract/150/23/234507/197649/Surface-tension-of-supercooled-water-nanodroplets?redirectedFrom=fulltext, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acs.jced.7b00519)
6) One other concern/issue that I have related to the first point is the role of NQEs (nuclear quantum effects) on the apparent anomalies which may become more enhance under supercooling.

### Reviewer 4

The authors study the temperature-dependence of the water-vapor interfacial tension using molecular dynamics simulations deep into the supercooled regime. The observed non-linear behavior including two inflection points is rationalized in terms of the competition of two distinct water populations (tetrahedral vs. random), of which the composition at the interface (and in bulk) changes with temperature. The surface tension profile agrees well with the differences in water ordering, thus the authors conclude that the competition between dipolar ordering and tetrahedral structure formation governs the resulting surface tension.
This conclusion is appealing since it rationalizes important aspects of water’s anomalies merely in terms of structural properties, while also not contradicting thermodynamic arguments involving a liquid-liquid critical point. The topic is of high interest and well written, however, especially the second half of the discussion (after the discussion of Figure 3) is very technical. While personally I find all points generally interesting and relevant, I am not sure if this is too detailed for the general audience of Nature Communications and thus the manuscript in its present form might be better suited for a more specialized journal.

- the inflection points in Fig1a are barely visible, maybe they could be indicated with arrows?

- Fig.3 d,e are not clear, what message should be taken here?
- detection of ice0-like structures: the manuscript should stand on its own and therefore at least briefly outline how these structures are detected. The same applies to the m-membered rings.
